messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Phommasack is a thirty-five-year-old Lao-American accountant who presented for an initial intake following a referral from his primary care physician, who had noted significant sleep disturbance and social withdrawal during a routine appointment. Kiet's PCL-5 score of 57 places him firmly within the severe range for post-traumatic stress, and the picture that emerged across the first two sessions was one of a man whose inner life had been quietly dismantled over the course of several years.

Kiet was detained by government authorities during a visit to his country of origin approximately four years ago. Over a period of several days, he was subjected to systematic physical and psychological torture — restrained, beaten, subjected to prolonged isolation, and interrogated by men whose faces he never clearly saw. What he remembers most vividly is not a single moment but a texture: the smell of the room, the sound of a door being unlocked, the feeling of not knowing whether the next person to enter would bring food or further harm. He was eventually released without explanation and returned to the United States, where he attempted to resume his life.

For a time, he managed. He returned to his position at a mid-sized accounting firm, filed his reports, attended his meetings. But the memories did not recede. They began arriving unbidden — not as ordinary recollections but as fragments that felt disordered and uncontrollable, a film that played over and over without his consent, cutting between images that he could not arrange into a coherent sequence. He found it impossible to say with confidence what had happened first, or second, or last. More unsettling still was the quality of dissociation that accompanied these intrusions: the memories felt as though they belonged to someone else, as though he were reviewing footage of a stranger's suffering rather than his own. This strangeness did not comfort him — it frightened him, because it confirmed what he had begun to suspect: that he had been permanently changed for the worse, that the person who had boarded the plane for that visit no longer existed.

It was in the ordinary machinery of his workday that the triggers became impossible to ignore. His role as an accountant required him to interact regularly with new clients — strangers, by definition — and each such encounter activated a vigilance he could not suppress. Talking to someone he did not know, someone whose intentions he could not verify, would bring the memory flooding back without warning: the guards, the interrogators, men who had offered nothing in their faces to read. These intrusions, arriving in the middle of a client meeting or a phone call, sharpened into the conviction that you can never truly know who will harm you — that any stranger might be concealing the same capacity for cruelty he had encountered in that room. The triggers did not merely recall the past; they reorganised his understanding of the present, feeding directly into a settled belief that the world was populated by unpredictable danger and that he himself was too damaged to navigate it safely. He had come to believe that someone stronger, more capable, would have found a way to stop what happened — a thought that returned whenever he caught himself flinching at a colleague's raised voice or freezing at the sound of a door.

These appraisals — of permanent damage, of inexplicable personal failure, of a world in which harm could come from any direction — did not remain abstract. They functioned as a lens through which the memories themselves were re-entered. When Kiet found himself believing, again, that he was irreparably broken, the looping film would begin to play: the restraints, the disorientation, the faces he could not see clearly, the sequence he could not reconstruct. Talking about the future, even in passing — a colleague mentioning a project timeline, a friend asking about plans — could set the same cycle in motion, as though the future itself had become a threatening unknown.

Kiet divorced two years ago. His former wife has said he became unreachable. He has reduced his client-facing responsibilities at work, citing administrative priorities, though he knows the real reason. What finally brought him to seek help was a performance review in which his supervisor noted his increasing withdrawal. He arrived at the intake session composed but exhausted, and what he said he wanted most was to stop feeling like a stranger to himself.
